articleHtml:
By Sarah Jenkins, CPA, Payroll & Tax Accounting Specialist · Tax year 2026 · Last updated: November 27, 2026

Start with the paycheck, not the formula

A salary offer is a gross number. What reaches your bank account is smaller, and by how much depends on your filing status, retirement contributions, state and a few payroll rules that most people never see broken down. The calculator above does the arithmetic. This page explains each step so you can sanity-check any result, including the ones from your employer's payroll system.

Worked example: a $75,000 salary, single filer, 2026

The figures below use 2026 federal rules for a single filer with no other income and no state tax.

StepAmount
Gross salary$75,000.00
Standard deduction (single, 2026)−$16,100.00
Taxable income$58,900.00
Federal income tax (see bracket math below)$7,670.00
Social Security, 6.2%$4,650.00
Medicare, 1.45%$1,087.50
Take-home (before state tax)$61,592.50
Per month / per bi-weekly check$5,132.71 / $2,368.94

The federal tax comes from the 2026 brackets for single filers: 10% on the first $12,400 ($1,240), 12% on the next $38,000 up to $50,400 ($4,560), and 22% on the remaining $8,500 ($1,870). Total: $7,670. Your effective federal rate is $7,670 ÷ $75,000 = 10.2%, even though you are "in the 22% bracket".

Marginal vs effective: why a raise never lowers your pay

Only the income inside a bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate. Crossing into the next bracket never reduces your take-home. Suppose you get a $5,000 raise, from $75,000 to $80,000. The extra income is taxed at 22% federal ($1,100) plus 7.65% payroll tax ($382.50). You keep $3,517.50 of the $5,000, about 70 cents on the dollar. That 70% is the number to use when comparing offers at the margin.

What pre-tax deductions really cost you

A traditional 401(k) contribution lowers federal taxable income, but not Social Security or Medicare tax. Contribute 6% ($4,500) and taxable income drops to $54,400. Federal tax falls to $6,680, a saving of $990. Take-home becomes $58,082.50, which is only $3,510 lower even though you put $4,500 into savings. Employer matching, if any, is extra on top.

Health insurance premiums paid through a payroll cafeteria plan and HSA contributions made through payroll can reduce both income tax and FICA. Check your pay stub to see which of your deductions are pre-tax.

Hourly, weekly and monthly conversions

The standard full-time year is 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks). A $75,000 salary is therefore about $36.06 per hour. Two caveats: unpaid time off changes the real figure, and monthly pay is annual ÷ 12 while bi-weekly pay is annual ÷ 26. In two months of the year a bi-weekly worker receives three checks, which is not extra income, just calendar timing.

High earners: the Social Security cap and Additional Medicare

Social Security tax stops once wages reach the annual wage base, $184,500 for 2026. After that point the 6.2% disappears from your checks. Medicare has no cap, and wages above $200,000 (single) add a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax. A few comparisons for a single filer taking the standard deduction, before state tax:

Bonuses: why they look smaller than expected

Employers generally withhold a flat 22% federal rate from a separately paid bonus, plus FICA. That is only withholding. Your actual tax is settled when you file, so if 22% was more than your real marginal rate you get it back as a refund, and if it was less you may owe a little.

What this calculator does not include

  • State and local income tax. Some states, such as Texas, Florida and Washington, do not tax wages; others, such as California and New York, can take several additional percent.
  • Credits such as the child tax credit or earned income credit.
  • Recent temporary deductions for items like qualified tips, overtime and seniors (running through 2028), which may apply to you.
  • Itemized deductions, if yours exceed the standard deduction.

Common mistakes

  • Multiplying your whole salary by your top bracket rate. Tax is progressive.
  • Assuming a 401(k) contribution reduces payroll tax. It does not.
  • Forgetting to update your W-4 after marriage, a second job or a new child.
  • Comparing a pre-tax salary in one state with a post-tax figure in another.

Frequently asked questions

How do I convert an hourly wage to an annual salary?

Multiply the hourly rate by hours per week and by 52. At 40 hours a week this equals the hourly rate × 2,080.

Why is my paycheck lower than this calculator shows?

Likely causes are state or local tax, health insurance premiums, retirement contributions, union dues or garnishments. Compare each line on your pay stub with the table above.

What is the difference between gross and net pay?

Gross pay is your total earnings before any deductions. Net pay, also called take-home pay, is what remains after taxes and deductions.

Does a higher tax bracket mean I earn less after a raise?

No. Only the portion of income above the bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so a raise always increases take-home pay.

Methodology and sources

Figures use the 2026 federal brackets, the 2026 standard deduction and the 2026 Social Security wage base as published by the IRS and Social Security Administration. The IRS has announced 2027 adjustments; this page will be updated when payroll tables switch. Estimates only, not tax advice. See IRS Publication 15-T for withholding methods.
